chapter.name: Geographical Diversity of India
chapter.blurb: The physical geography of India: boundaries, the Himalayas, plains, desert, plateau, coasts, islands and the Northeast.

concepts.name: India's location, boundaries and five regions
concepts.description: India as the seventh-largest country, the Indian Subcontinent, its natural boundaries and the five regions used to describe it.
concepts.idea: India's mountains, desert and seas form natural boundaries that shaped its climate, culture and history.
concepts.rule: India is the seventh-largest country and part of Asia. With Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, Sri Lanka and Myanmar it forms the Indian Subcontinent. The Himalayas lie in the north, the Thar Desert and Arabian Sea in the west, the Indian Ocean in the south and the Bay of Bengal in the east. Five regions are used: the great mountain zone, the plains of the Ganga and the Indus, the desert region, the southern peninsula and the islands.
concepts.example: The Himalayan range stands like a wall in the north of India.

questions.q: Why can a person not walk into India from the south, the way they can from the north?
questions.a: In the south lies the Indian Ocean, so the land ends at the sea, whereas the north is bounded by mountains.

questions.q: Compare how the north and the south of India are bounded.
questions.a: The north is bounded by the Himalayan mountain barrier, while the south is bounded by the Indian Ocean.

questions.q: Explain how India's geography gives it a distinct national character, as Sri Aurobindo suggests.
questions.a: Its mountains, desert and seas separate it from the rest of Asia, and these boundaries shaped its climate, culture and history, giving the country a distinct character.
s: They shaped climate, culture and history
Links to a distinct national character

questions.q: Is it right to say India is completely cut off from the rest of Asia? Justify with reasons.
questions.a: Not completely. The Himalayas, desert and seas create a separation, but India is part of Asia and forms the Indian Subcontinent with its neighbours.
s: Notes India is part of Asia and the subcontinent

questions.q: Describe a simple sketch map of India that shows the five regions and the boundaries.
questions.a: The sketch shows the Himalayas in the north, the plains below them, the Thar Desert in the west, the southern peninsula, the islands, and labels the Arabian Sea, Bay of Bengal and Indian Ocean.

concepts.name: The Himalayas: formation, ranges and importance
concepts.description: How the Himalayas were formed, their three ranges, Gaumukh and the Ganga, and why they matter.
concepts.idea: The Himalayas formed when India collided with Eurasia and are the water tower and a sacred home for millions.
concepts.rule: About 50 million years ago India, once part of Gondwana, collided with Eurasia and the land between crumpled upward. The mountains still rise about 5 mm a year. The three ranges are Himadri (Greater), Himachal (Lower) and the Shivalik Hills (Outer). Snowmelt feeds the Ganga, Indus and Brahmaputra, so the range is called the Water Tower of Asia. The Bhagirathi begins at Gaumukh in Uttarakhand.
concepts.example: Kath-kuni houses use local stone and wood to keep warm and resist mild earthquakes.

questions.q: Describe the three ranges of the Himalayas in order from north to south.
questions.a: The Himadri or Greater Himalayas are the highest, the Himachal or Lower Himalayas lie south of them, and the Shivalik Hills are the outermost and lowest range.

questions.a: the Himachal

questions.a: Himadri

questions.a: 5 mm x 1000 = 5000 mm, which is 5 metres.

questions.q: Why do the rivers Ganga and Indus keep flowing even in summer?
questions.a: In summer the snow on the mountains melts and feeds the rivers, so the Himalayas supply water all year.

questions.q: Why are kath-kuni houses suitable for the western Himalayas?

questions.q: A hiker starts at Gaumukh and follows the water downstream. Explain what river she is following and why the place is important.
questions.a: She follows the Bhagirathi, a major tributary of the Ganga, which begins at Gaumukh at the edge of the Gangotri Glacier. The place is sacred and attracts pilgrims and trekkers.

questions.q: Consider these statements about the Himalayas. (I) India was once part of a larger landmass called Gondwana. (II) Himalayan peaks over 8000 metres in height are together called the 'Seven Thousanders'. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Only I

questions.q: Explain how the Himalayas connect to the lives of hundreds of millions of people.
questions.a: Snowmelt feeds rivers that give water for drinking, farming and industry, and the mountains are also sacred to many cultures.
s: Rivers give water for drinking and farming

questions.q: Compare the Himadri and the Himachal in climate and human life.
questions.a: The Himadri is snow-covered all year with few settlements, while the Himachal has a milder climate with rich biodiversity, human habitation and hill stations.

questions.q: Is it fair to call the Himalayas a 'natural wall'? Support your answer.
questions.a: Partly yes, because the range is about 2500 km long and acts as a barrier in the north; but it is also a source of water and a place with people, monasteries and rivers flowing out of it.
s: Also a source of water and life

questions.q: Write a short story titled 'How I Was Born' from the point of view of the Himalayas.
questions.a: A story that includes India breaking from Gondwana, moving north, colliding with Eurasia about 50 million years ago, the land crumpling upward and the mountains still growing a little each year.

concepts.name: The cold desert of Ladakh and the Gangetic Plains
concepts.description: Ladakh as a cold desert with Pangong Tso and unique wildlife, and the fertile, densely populated Gangetic Plains.
concepts.idea: Ladakh is a high, dry cold desert; the plains fed by Himalayan rivers are fertile and support many people.
concepts.rule: Ladakh is a cold desert where winter temperatures fall below -30 degrees C, with little rain, rocky terrain and lakes such as Pangong Tso, a salty lake. Its landscape is called moonland. Yaks are reared for milk, meat, wool and dung and for transport. The Gangetic Plains, fed by the Ganga, Indus and Brahmaputra systems, have fertile soil, a large population and good road and rail networks.
concepts.example: Yaks in Ladakh give milk, meat, wool and dung and carry loads.

questions.q: Compare Ladakh and the Gangetic Plains in climate, land and population.
questions.a: Ladakh is cold and dry with rugged land and few people, while the Gangetic Plains are fertile and flat with a large population.

questions.q: Explain how the mountains, rivers and plains are connected in the story of the Gangetic Plains.
questions.a: Rivers rising in the Himalayas carry water and minerals to the plains, enriching the soil and supporting agriculture, settlements, transport and civilisation.

questions.q: Which is a better place to live, Ladakh or the Gangetic Plains? Give reasons.
questions.a: The Gangetic Plains have fertile land, water and transport for many people, whereas Ladakh has harsh cold and little rain, though it has unique culture and wildlife. Reasons are supported with facts.

questions.q: Design a poster for tourists that promotes Ladakh and mentions its unique features.
questions.a: The poster shows moonland scenery, Pangong Tso, snow leopards, ibex and Tibetan antelopes, monasteries and festivals such as Losar and the Hemis Festival.

concepts.name: The Thar Desert and the Aravalli Hills
concepts.description: The Thar Desert's sand dunes, harsh conditions and water conservation, and the ancient Aravalli Hills.
concepts.idea: People adapt to the Thar's harsh climate, while the ancient Aravallis limit the desert's spread and hold minerals.
concepts.rule: The Thar is a vast arid region across Rajasthan, Gujarat, Punjab and Haryana with dunes up to 150 metres high, very hot days and cold nights. Rajasthan conserves water through taanka or kunds. The Aravalli Hills are about 2.5 billion years old, act as a natural barrier stopping the Thar from spreading east, and are rich in marble, granite, zinc and copper. Zawar mines show early zinc extraction.
concepts.example: Women in the desert clean utensils with sand and reuse the rinse water.

questions.a: They act as a natural barrier that stops the Thar from spreading east and shape the climate of the region, and they hold minerals.

questions.q: Compare how people live in the Thar and near the Aravallis, using the chapter's facts.
questions.a: Thar people adapt to heat and scarce water with sand-cleaning and taanka, while the Aravallis support mining, construction and forts like Chittorgarh and Kumbhalgarh.

questions.q: 'The desert is an empty and lifeless place.' Do you agree? Give reasons.
questions.a: No. People have adapted their food, clothing and lifestyle, there is wildlife such as the peacock and gharial elsewhere in the region, and cities like Jaisalmer thrive.

questions.q: Write a slogan and three tips for saving water inspired by the people of the Thar.
questions.a: A slogan about every drop counting, and tips such as reusing rinse water for plants, harvesting rain and not leaving taps running.

concepts.name: The Peninsular Plateau
concepts.description: The triangular plateau, the Western and Eastern Ghats, the Deccan Plateau and the rivers, forests, minerals and tribal communities.
concepts.idea: The old, mineral-rich Peninsular Plateau, bordered by the Ghats, drains through rivers flowing east and west.
concepts.rule: The Peninsular Plateau is a very old, triangular landform surrounded by water on three sides. It is bordered by the taller Western Ghats (also the Sahyadri in the north) and the lower, broken Eastern Ghats, with the Deccan Plateau between. The Godavari, Krishna, Mahanadi and Kaveri flow east; the Narmada and Tapti flow west. The plateau is rich in minerals and forests and is home to tribal communities such as the Santhal, Gond, Baiga, Bhil and Korku.
concepts.example: Rivers that flow over uneven plateau rock create waterfalls used for hydroelectric power.

questions.q: Explain how the plateau's location, rivers and minerals together matter to the country.
questions.a: Being an old landform between the Ghats, the plateau's rivers give water for farming, industry and power, and its minerals and forests support the economy.

questions.q: Is the Western Ghats' UNESCO status justified? Give two reasons.

concepts.name: Coasts, islands, the Sundarbans and the hills of the Northeast
concepts.description: India's 7500 km coastline, the west and east coasts, deltas, Lakshadweep, Andaman and Nicobar, the Sundarbans and the Meghalaya hills.
concepts.idea: India's varied coasts, islands, delta and northeastern hills show the variety of its geography.
concepts.rule: The coastline is over 7500 km long. The west coast runs from Gujarat to Kerala with estuaries at the Narmada and Tapti. The east coast lies between the Eastern Ghats and the Bay of Bengal with wide plains and deltas of the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri, and lakes such as Chilika and Pulicat. Lakshadweep has 36 coral islands; the Andaman and Nicobar islands are volcanic, with Barren Island the only active volcano. The Sundarbans lie in the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta. The Meghalaya Plateau has heavy rainfall.
concepts.example: A delta forms when a river deposits sediments at its mouth and builds a triangular area.
